title: Vanguard just scored a $4-billion private placement to close its $4.6-billion Altruist deal by year's end, but it comes with at least a $200-million annual drag on its legendary at-cost model

 Expert voice Got a tip? Vanguard just scored a $4-billion private placement to close its $4.6-billion Altruist deal by year's end, but it comes with at least a $200-million annual drag on its legendary at-cost model
 The giant Malvern company is apparently set to close in 2026, though it needed Bank of America, Citigroup Inc. and JPMorgan Chase & Co. to broker a private placement to fund the deal.
 6 min read By Brooke Southall November 10, 2026 Salim Ramji, Jason Wenk (r): We’ve had the benefit of getting to get to know Altruist’s people, platform, and potential. Key Points Vanguard secured a $4-billion private placement to finalize its $4.6-billion acquisition of RIA custodian Altruist by year-end.
 Interest payments on the debt could exceed $200 million annually, potentially pressuring Vanguard's traditional at-cost business model.
 Altruist provides Vanguard a modern, AI-enabled platform to compete against legacy RIA custody leaders like Schwab and Fidelity.
 Industry analysts suggest the deal incentivizes asset managers to shift assets toward Altruist to avoid competitor platform fees.
 AI generated Brooke's Note: What struck me as I wrote this article about Vanguard getting locked and loaded with funding to buy Altruist is just how determined it needs to be to make RIA custody happen. Yes, $4 billion is lots of money. But so are the hundreds of millions it will need to pay in interest on the capital — $200 million or more. Vanguard is not simply deploying cash sitting idly on its balance sheet. For now, those private placement borrowing costs will need to be funded by something other than Altruist, which is not currently known to be cash flow positive. In other words, Vanguard is launching its RIA strategy with a big downside if its execution doesn't go according to plan. That's scary. It's also the oldest, best reason I've heard yet about why Vanguard may succeed in RIA custody. Failure really isn't much of an option. 
 Vanguard Group's $4-billion private placement deal will give it the liquidity to close its Altruist acquisition by year's end, but the money won't come cheap and raises questions about how it will affect investors and Vanguard's bottom line. 
 The funding – brokered by Citi, JPMorgan and Bank of America and revealed by Bloomberg today (Nov. 10) – probably has Vanguard on the hook annually for $200 million or more of interest payments alone, if it's paying the prevailing rate of 5% to 7%. 
 High-grade private placements carry an illiquidity premium of 150 to 250 basis points (bps) over public equivalents, according to financial references. The U.S. 10-Year Treasury Note currently trades at 4.90% to 5.00%
 For Vanguard , $4 billion is hardly pocket change. Its $13 trillion in managed assets generate about $9 billion in revenue annually, based on an average fee of 0.07%. Its cash flow is a fraction of that amount.
 Unanswered for the moment is how Vanguard 's investor-owners will be affected by the placement. Vanguard traditionally has plowed profits back into the company to lower fees, raising a question: Will Vanguard now have to raise fees to cover the debt service?
 Maybe there are no “external shareholders,” but now a host of external Altruist debt holders will expect to get their $4 billion back, with interest, whether the deal works out or not. 
 Vanguard declined to comment to Bloomberg, and RIABiz has a late-day query with Vanguard. Our query also asked if the closing is still slated for 2026.
 AI advantage
 Altruist is a small RIA custodian that does not charge fees but scrapes revenue through traditional means like interest on cash deposits, mutual fund revenue sharing, and interest on margin lending, its website says. It will operate as a “standalone” business under Vanguard and the company hasn't yet outlined how its profits will be returned to investors over time.
 But Altruist could plump Vanguard profit margins if Altruist RIAs emphasize Vanguard funds in their portfolios. Vanguard has been bolstering its model portfolio program while entering the custody business. See: Salim Ramji (strategically) bends to the will of RIAs by allowing them latitude to remodel Vanguard model portfolios and let three favorite RIA partners -- Orion, Black Diamond and Vestmark — get a cut of the action 
 Though many industry observers presumed that the RIA custody ship had sailed for Vanguard , it saw an opportunity to steal a march with the advent of AI. Schwab Advisor Services has struggled to retrofit its legacy RIA platform with artificial intelligence and has been forced to enter cautiously. Its two big partnerships – with Anthropic and Nevis – initially created excitement but were subsequently revealed to be limited to read-only functions. 
 Vanguard never revealed Altruist 's valuation. Off-record reports pegged it at $4.6 billion. Vanguard also never said how it would muster the cash at closing, though it promised to do so by year-end 2026. Though $4 billion is less than the reported price, Vanguard already holds a substantial stake, having invested seed capital as far back as 2020.
 Mission-aligned
 Vanguard's push into financial advice also gained momentum when it hired Salim Ramji from BlackRock as CEO in July of 2024. At the time of the Altruist deal on Aug. 26 this year, he described it as a “significant opportunity.” 
 “We’ve had the benefit of getting to get to know Altruist ’s people, platform, and potential over the last several years, and what we saw was a mission-aligned organization building AI-enabled technology around the real needs of advisors and the investors they serve,” he s
 Michael Kitces : I don't think it's a coincidence that Vanguard chose now to take action. aid.
 “As more investors in Vanguard funds choose to work with financial advisors, we see a significant opportunity to build on the strengths of two highly complementary organizations to help advisors serve clients more effectively and help more investors achieve financial security and peace of mind.”
 Of course with Vanguard , there is always a pricing angle. Michael Kitces , co-founder of XY Planning, a RIA network that uses Vanguard funds and both Altruist and Schwab's RIA custody, sees the value in a Vanguard-Altruist play.
 Advisor shift
 “I don't think it's a coincidence that Vanguard chose now to take action, after a 50-year history of not being in RIA custody,” he said in an earlier RIABiz email exchange. See: Vanguard struck with Altruist take-out after Schwab (and Fidelity) zapped it with ETF 'platform' fees, lightning bolts that clearly woke a sleeping monster that could redraw the competitive landscape for RIA custody, with massive 'Vanguard effect,' analysts say 
 " Altruist becomes not just the de facto platform of choice for advisors using very-popular Vanguard funds (and perhaps DFA/Avantis that also fought the pay-to-play battle with custodians), but now all asset managers have an incentive to see advisors shift from Schwab and Fidelity to Vanguard's Altruist .
 “NO asset manager wants to have to increase the expense ratios of their own ETFs (and debit their own performance track record) to pay Schwab / Fidelity platform fees.
 “So now Vanguard 's Altruist may have... every asset manager wholesaler in the country lobbying for Altruist to take RIA market share to keep their own costs down. 
 "Oh, and Vanguard 's Altruist can do it all at lower cost for themselves, too, because it doesn't have external shareholders to drive profits towards, thanks to Vanguard's legendary ownership structure?”
